<content>
<para id="import-auto-id1596511">Which weighs more, a ton of feathers or a ton of bricks? This old riddle plays with the distinction between mass and density. A ton is a ton, of course; but bricks have much greater density than feathers, and so we are tempted to think of them as heavier. (See <link target-id="import-auto-id950378"/>.)</para>
    <para id="import-auto-id3217118"><term id="import-auto-id2660162">Density</term>, as you will see, is an important characteristic of substances. It is crucial, for example, in determining whether an object sinks or floats in a fluid. Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance or object. In equation form, density is defined as</para>
    <equation id="eip-385"><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mfrac><m:mi>m</m:mi><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mfrac></m:mrow><m:mo>,</m:mo></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ= {  {m}  over  {V} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math></equation><para id="import-auto-id2677741">where the Greek letter <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> (rho) is the symbol for density, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>m</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{m} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the mass, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{V} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the volume occupied by the substance. </para>
    <note id="fs-id3045369"><label/>
    <title>Density</title>
    <para id="import-auto-id1412810">Density is mass per unit volume.</para>
    <equation id="eip-462"><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mfrac><m:mi>m</m:mi><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mfrac></m:mrow><m:mo>,</m:mo></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ= {  {m}  over  {V} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math></equation><para id="import-auto-id2621355">where <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the symbol for density, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>m</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{m} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the mass, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{V} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the volume occupied by the substance. </para>
    </note>
    <para id="import-auto-id1011172">In the riddle regarding the feathers and bricks, the masses are the same, but the volume occupied by the feathers is much greater, since their density is much lower. The SI unit of density is <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>kg/m</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"kg/m" rSup { size 8{3} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, representative values are given in <link target-id="fs-id1769034"/>. The metric system was originally devised so that water would have a density of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:msup><m:mtext>g/cm</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{1`"g/cm" rSup { size 8{3} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, equivalent to <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:msup><m:mtext>kg/m</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"10" rSup { size 8{3} } `"kg/m" rSup { size 8{3} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>. Thus the basic mass unit, the kilogram, was first devised to be the mass of 1000 mL of water, which has a volume of 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>.</para><table id="fs-id1769034" summary="The table shows the value of density in units of kilogram per meter cubed for certain solids, liquids, and gases."><title>Densities of Various Substances</title>

<content>
<para id="import-auto-id1596511">Which weighs more, a ton of feathers or a ton of bricks? This old riddle plays with the distinction between mass and density. A ton is a ton, of course; but bricks have much greater density than feathers, and so we are tempted to think of them as heavier. (See <link target-id="import-auto-id950378"/>.)</para>
    <para id="import-auto-id3217118"><term id="import-auto-id2660162">Density</term>, as you will see, is an important characteristic of substances. It is crucial, for example, in determining whether an object sinks or floats in a fluid. Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance or object. In equation form, density is defined as</para>
    <equation id="eip-385"><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mfrac><m:mi>m</m:mi><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mfrac></m:mrow><m:mo>,</m:mo></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ= {  {m}  over  {V} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math></equation><para id="import-auto-id2677741">where the Greek letter <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> (rho) is the symbol for density, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>m</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{m} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the mass, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{V} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the volume occupied by the substance. </para>
    <note id="fs-id3045369"><label/>
    <title>Density</title>
    <para id="import-auto-id1412810">Density is mass per unit volume.</para>
    <equation id="eip-462"><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mfrac><m:mi>m</m:mi><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mfrac></m:mrow><m:mo>,</m:mo></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ= {  {m}  over  {V} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math></equation><para id="import-auto-id2621355">where <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>ρ</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ρ} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the symbol for density, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>m</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{m} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the mass, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>V</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{V} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the volume occupied by the substance. </para>
    </note>
    <para id="import-auto-id1011172">In the riddle regarding the feathers and bricks, the masses are the same, but the volume occupied by the feathers is much greater, since their density is much lower. The SI unit of density is <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>kg/m</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"kg/m" rSup { size 8{3} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, representative values are given in <link target-id="fs-id1769034"/>. The metric system was originally devised so that water would have a density of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:msup><m:mtext>g/cm</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{1`"g/cm" rSup { size 8{3} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, equivalent to <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:msup><m:mtext>kg/m</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"10" rSup { size 8{3} } `"kg/m" rSup { size 8{3} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>.     <caption>A ton of feathers and a ton of bricks have the same mass, but the feathers make a much bigger pile because they have a much lower density.</caption></figure><para id="import-auto-id1418776">As you can see by examining <link target-id="fs-id1769034"/>, the density of an object may help identify its composition. The density of gold, for example, is about 2.5 times the density of iron, which is about 2.5 times the density of aluminum. Density also reveals something about the phase of the matter and its substructure. Notice that the densities of liquids and solids are roughly comparable, consistent with the fact that their atoms are in close contact. The densities of gases are much less than those of liquids and solids, because the atoms in gases are separated by large amounts of empty space.</para><note id="fs-id2971617"><label/>

    <para id="import-auto-id1381758">A pile of sugar and a pile of salt look pretty similar, but which weighs more? What values did you find? What method did you use to determine these values?</para>

    <example id="fs-id2449267">
    <title>Calculating the Mass of a Reservoir From Its Volume</title>
